title: Module 7: High Availability & Replication
content: Ensuring 24/7 Uptime with AMPS 🛡️
Understanding Replication and Failover
speakerNotes: Welcome to Module 7. Today we're diving into the 'heart' of AMPS reliability: High Availability and Replication.

title: Why High Availability?
content: Hardware fails, networks glitch, and sites go dark. 💥
Business-critical data needs to be available regardless.
AMPS provides 'Always On' capabilities through:
- Persistent Transaction Logging 📜
- Real-time Integrated Replication 🔄
- Automatic Client Failover ⚡
speakerNotes: High availability isn't just about the server; it's about the entire ecosystem working together to mask failures from the end-user.

title: The Core Architecture: Peer-to-Peer
content: No single point of failure (No controller/quorum nodes).
Leaderless: Every node is 'hot' and processes independently. 🔥
Replication is point-to-point and unidirectional by default.
Bidirectional replication creates a Hot-Hot pair.
speakerNotes: Unlike some systems that rely on a central 'zoo-keeper' or 'orchestrator', AMPS nodes are independent peers. This simplifies deployment and increases resilience.

title: Replication Topologies: Pair (Hot-Hot)
content: Standard failover configuration.
Two instances (Group A) replicating to each other.
Clients can connect to either instance.
mermaid:
graph LR
  A[Instance 1] <-->|Sync Replication| B[Instance 2]
  C[Client] --> A
  C -.->|Failover| B
speakerNotes: The Pair topology is the bread and butter of AMPS HA. Usually configured with Synchronous replication.

title: Replication Topologies: Hub and Spoke (Star)
content: Scaling out to hundreds of downstream consumers.
Ingestion Tier -> Hub Tier -> Application Tier.
Hubs act as pure distributors (no SOW, usually).
mermaid:
graph LR
  I[Ingestion] --> H[Hub]
  H --> S1[Spoke 1]
  H --> S2[Spoke 2]
  H --> S3[Spoke 3]
speakerNotes: Hub and Spoke is ideal for distributing data to different regions or departments without putting load on the ingestion servers.

title: Replication Topologies: Mesh
content: Highly interconnected network.
Uses PassThrough replication to forward data.
Multiple paths for redundancy. 🕸️
mermaid:
graph TD
  A <--> B
  B <--> C
  C <--> A
  A <--> D
  D <--> B
speakerNotes: Mesh topologies provide maximum redundancy but require careful configuration of PassThrough rules to avoid infinite loops.

title: Sync vs. Async Replication
content: **Sync (Synchronous):** 🤝
- Publisher waits for ACK from ALL sync destinations.
- Zero data loss guarantee during failover.
**Async (Asynchronous):** 🚀
- Publisher gets ACK as soon as the message is local.
- High performance, suitable for DR sites.
speakerNotes: Choose Sync for local HA pairs and Async for remote Disaster Recovery sites where latency might be high.

title: Failover: The 'Self-Healing' Instance
content: AMPS instances are aware of what they've missed.
**Resynchronization (Resync):** On reconnect, the source replays missed journals.
Uses `/AMPS/Tx/Checkpoint` to find the exact restart point.
Ensures the transaction log is eventually consistent. 🩹
speakerNotes: Resync happens automatically. You don't need to manually restore backups or 'sync' files.

title: Client Failover: HAClient
content: The AMPS Client Libraries (Java, C++, Python, etc.) handle the heavy lifting.
**HAClient Features:**
- Automatic Reconnection.
- Subscription Recovery.
- Duplicate Suppression using Sequence Numbers.
speakerNotes: By using the HAClient class, your application code stays simple while AMPS manages the network complexity.

title: Bookmark Subscriptions: Resume Anywhere
content: Subscriptions can survive both client and server restarts.
Client stores the last seen 'Bookmark'.
On reconnect, client says: 'Start from Bookmark X'.
AMPS replays exactly what was missed. 📑
speakerNotes: Bookmarks are the key to durable subscriptions. They work across any instance in the replication group.

title: Transactional Integrity: Sequence Numbers
content: Every message has a **Client Name** + **Sequence Number**.
Prevents duplicates if a publisher resends during failover.
AMPS 'Duplicate Detection' ensures one record in the SOW. ✅
speakerNotes: Sequence numbers ensure that even if a publisher 'blindly' resends, the system stays consistent.

title: Replicating the SOW
content: SOW caches are replicated command-by-command.
Replicates `publish`, `delta_publish`, and `sow_delete`.
Ensures real-time query results are identical on all nodes. 📂
speakerNotes: When you update a SOW record, the 'delta' or 'publish' is sent across the wire, updating all mirrored SOW files.

title: Replicating Queues: Ownership
content: Queues are tricky: Only one person can process a message! ☝️
**Message Ownership:** The instance that received the publish 'owns' the message.
Only the owner delivers to its local subscribers.
Other nodes can 'request' ownership if they have idle workers.
speakerNotes: Queue replication ensures that delivery guarantees are maintained even in a distributed cluster.

title: Disaster Recovery: Proxied Transfer
content: What if the owner of a queue message goes offline? 😱
**Proxied Transfer:** Allows another instance to 'proxy' the ownership.
Ensures queue messages don't get 'stuck' on a dead server.
Used for temporary recovery during site failures.
speakerNotes: Proxied transfer is a powerful DR tool for queues, allowing work to continue even if the original ingestion site is gone.

title: Best Practices for HA
content: 1. Always use unique **Client Names**. 🆔
2. Use **Sync** replication for failover partners.
3. Enable **PassThrough** for cluster-wide visibility.
4. Monitor your replication latency using the Admin console. 📊
speakerNotes: Following these rules will save you from common headaches like message loss or split-brain scenarios.
